claim: Neurons communicate by the activity-dependent release of small-molecule neurotransmitters packaged into synaptic vesicles (SVs).
source: Neurons communicate by the activity-dependent release of small-molecule neurotransmitters packaged into synaptic vesicles (SVs).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in neuroscience supported by extensive literature and represents foundational knowledge in the field.

claim: Technical limitations have precluded a full metabolomic analysis of SV content.
source: Although many molecules have been identified as neurotransmitters, technical limitations have precluded a full metabolomic analysis of SV content.
evidence: The authors state this as a motivation for their work, representing their assessment of the current state of the field.

claim: The only detectable polar metabolites in SVs isolated from primary cortical neurons are the established neurotransmitters glutamate and GABA.
source: Unbiased and extensive global profiling of SVs isolated from these neurons revealed that the only detectable polar metabolites they contain are the established neurotransmitters glutamate and GABA.
evidence: This claim is supported by the global metabolomics data presented in Figure 3 and described in the Results section.

claim: SVs rapidly fuse with the membrane to release their neurotransmitters upon electrical excitation of a neuron via action potentials.
source: Upon electrical excitation of a neuron via action potentials, SVs rapidly fuse with the membrane to release their neurotransmitters, which are detected by transmembrane receptors on a postsynaptic neuron (Südhof, 2013; Traynelis et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature in the field.

claim: The functional contribution of a neuron to a circuit is defined by the neurotransmitters it releases and the postsynaptic cells that it contacts.
source: Thus, the functional contribution of a neuron to a circuit is defined by the neurotransmitters it releases and the postsynaptic cells that it contacts.
evidence: This is a logical conclusion drawn from the preceding discussion about neurotransmitter function and represents established understanding in neuroscience.

claim: Neurons were classically believed to release only one fast-acting neurotransmitter, whose identity was fixed throughout the lifetime of the neuron.
source: Neurons were classically believed to release only one fast-acting neurotransmitter, whose identity was fixed throughout the lifetime of the neuron (Strata and Harvey, 1999).
evidence: This historical perspective is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Neurons in many brain regions have recently been discovered to release multiple neurotransmitters.
source: However, neurons in many brain regions have recently been discovered to release multiple neurotransmitters (Hnasko and Edwards, 2012; Jonas et al., 1998; Root et al., 2014; Shabel et al., 2014; Tritsch et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to recent research findings.

claim: Neurons in the developing and mature brain have been found to lose, add, or switch the neurotransmitters they release in an activity-dependent manner.
source: In addition, neurons in the developing and mature brain have been found to lose, add, or switch the neurotransmitters they release in an activity-dependent manner (Dulcis et al., 2013; Spitzer, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Current protocols for SV purification are optimized for proteomic characterizations and require several hours to days to complete.
source: However, current protocols are optimized for proteomic characterizations of SVs and require several hours to days to complete, during which the activity of transporters and biosynthetic enzymes may alter the contents of purified SVs (Ahmed et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and represents a limitation of existing methods that the authors aim to address.

claim: The activity of transporters and biosynthetic enzymes may alter the contents of purified SVs during lengthy purification protocols.
source: However, current protocols are optimized for proteomic characterizations of SVs and require several hours to days to complete, during which the activity of transporters and biosynthetic enzymes may alter the contents of purified SVs (Ahmed et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative concern based on the time required for existing protocols, supported by citations.

claim: A method was developed to rapidly immunopurify SVs from both cultured mouse neurons and intact mouse brains within half an hour.
source: To overcome these caveats, we developed a method to rapidly immunopurify SVs from both cultured mouse neurons and intact mouse brains within half an hour.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the detailed methods and results presented.

claim: The expression of SV-tag did not alter glutamate release from cultured mouse cortical neurons.
source: In cultured mouse cortical neurons, the expression of SV-tag did not alter glutamate release from these cells, as determined by recording spontaneous miniature excitatory post-synaptic currents (mEPSCs) at a holding potential of −70 mV in the presence of TTX and gabazine (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Synaptophysin is an SV-specific, integral membrane protein that is ubiquitously present and highly abundant on SVs.
source: We developed SV-tag, a construct in which a hemagglutinin (HA) tag is fused to the C-terminus of synaptophysin, an SV-specific, integral membrane protein and an ideal candidate to tag due to its ubiquitous presence and high abundance on SVs (Figure 1A; Takamori et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to established literature characterizing synaptophysin.

claim: ATP was added throughout the purification to maintain vATPase function, which establishes the proton gradient across the SV membrane necessary for the import of neurotransmitters.
source: ATP was added throughout the purification to maintain vATPase function, which establishes the proton gradient across the SV membrane that is necessary for the import of neurotransmitters and the maintenance of their levels within SVs (Burger et al., 1989).
evidence: This methodological detail is supported by a citation explaining the role of vATPase.

claim: The majority of particles isolated from the workflow are spheres of ~40–70 nm in diameter, as expected for SVs.
source: Furthermore, transmission electron microscopy revealed that the majority of particles isolated from our workflow are spheres of ~40–70 nm in diameter (Eshkind and Leube, 1995), as expected for SVs (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, with a citation for the expected size range.

claim: SVs isolated with SV-tag are comparable to those purified via lengthier, traditional differential centrifugation protocols, as assessed by immunoblot and electron microscopy.
source: Finally, SVs isolated with SV-tag are comparable to those purified via lengthier, traditional differential centrifugation protocols, as assessed by immunoblot (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H) and electron microscopy (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I), albeit with a reduction in yield that comes as a tradeoff for the speed of isolation.
evidence: This comparison is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H and 1I.

claim: The yield of SVs from the workflow is approximately 1.5% based on three SV markers.
source: Based on three SV markers, our yields were ~1.5% (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G), which is consistent with previous rapid organellar isolations (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This quantitative finding is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and compared to a cited reference.

claim: The SV preparations are 10-fold enriched in SVs, as based on synaptobrevin quantification.
source: Furthermore, we performed quantitative immunoblotting to determine that our preps were 10-fold enriched in SVs, as based on synaptobrevin (Figure 1H).
evidence: This quantitative measurement is supported by data presented in Figure 1H.

claim: Glutamate was enriched in isolated SVs compared to the material obtained when the same protocol was applied to uninfected neurons.
source: Using a luminescence-based assay to detect glutamate, we observed an enrichment of glutamate in isolated SVs compared to the material obtained when the same protocol was applied to uninfected neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This finding is supported by luminescence assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1J.

claim: Glutamate was depleted from SVs upon treatment of neurons with BafilomycinA, a vATPase inhibitor.
source: Importantly, glutamate was depleted upon treatment of neurons with BafilomycinA (BafA), a vATPase inhibitor that dissipates the proton gradient of SVs that is essential for the import of glutamate into SVs (Bowman et al., 1988).
evidence: This experimental result is supported by a citation explaining the mechanism of BafilomycinA.

claim: In primary cortical cultures, glutamate was the sole metabolite that was significantly enriched in SVs when compared to control.
source: In primary cortical cultures, glutamate was the sole metabolite that was significantly enriched in SVs when compared to control (Figure 2A) and it was the only metabolite depleted by BafA treatment (Figure 2B), consistent with the excitatory and glutamatergic identity of these neurons.
evidence: This finding is supported by GC/MS data presented in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Non-neurotransmitter amino acids were not enriched in SV preparations, demonstrating high purity.
source: Importantly, non-neurotransmitter amino acids were not enriched, demonstrating that our SV preparations are of high purity as they lack contaminating metabolites.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the metabolomics data showing selective enrichment of neurotransmitters.

claim: Aspartate was not detected in SVs from primary cortical cultures, suggesting that it does not function as a neurotransmitter in these cells.
source: Of note, aspartate was not detected in these vesicles, suggesting that it does not function as a neurotransmitter in these cells. The same conclusion was reached via electrophysiological studies for hippocampal excitatory synapses (Herring et al., 2015).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the absence of aspartate in the metabolomics data and is supported by a citation to corroborating electrophysiological studies.

claim: SVs isolated from MGE cells are enriched for GABA but not glutamate.
source: Reflecting the differences in the neurotransmitter identities of cortical and MGE-derived neurons, GC/MS analysis revealed that SVs isolated from MGE cells are enriched for GABA but not glutamate, whereas the converse is observed for cortical cultures (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This finding is supported by GC/MS data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Glutamate was the sole detected metabolite that is significantly enriched within SV-tag isolated SVs in LC/MS analysis.
source: Corroborating our earlier findings with GC/MS, glutamate was the sole detected metabolite that is significantly enriched within SV-tag isolated SVs (Figure 2C) and depleted upon BafA treatment (Figure 2D; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This finding is supported by LC/MS data presented in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: Markers for other subcellular compartments were not enriched in SV preparations, including cystine (lysosomes), aspartate and phosphocholine (mitochondria).
source: Reflecting the specificity of our workflow for isolating SVs, markers for other subcellular compartments were not enriched, including cystine, which is characteristic of lysosomes (Pisoni and Thoene, 1991), and aspartate and phosphocholine, which are the most enriched metabolites in mitochondria (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the metabolomics data and is supported by citations identifying these metabolites as markers for specific organelles.

claim: CRISPR-mediated depletion of VGLUT1 and VGLUT2 from cortical neurons significantly reduced glutamate levels from isolated SVs.
source: Reassuringly, CRISPR-mediated depletion of these transporters from cortical neurons by targeting the genes Slc17a6 (VGLUT2) and Slc17a7 (VGLUT1) significantly reduced glutamate levels from isolated SVs (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This experimental result is supported by data presented in Figure 2E and F.

claim: Global metabolomics screen detected 2724 representative features in SVs.
source: Overall, we detected 2724 representative features which were defined by an observed m/z (25 ppm) at a specific retention time (±0.25 min) with a minimum intensity and signal to noise threshold (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the global metabolomics analysis.

claim: Only three metabolites satisfied the criteria of being significantly enriched in SVs and concomitantly depleted by BafA: glutamate, GABA, and potassium.
source: To our surprise, only three metabolites satisfied these criteria – glutamate, GABA, and potassium (Figure 3C, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This finding is supported by the global metabolomics data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: GABA in cortical culture SVs likely originates from a minority population of interneurons.
source: In these samples, GABA likely originates from a minority population of interneurons in cultured cortical neurons, consistent with the low expression level of VGAT, the GABA transporter, observed in these cultures (Figure S2B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the detection of GABA and the known composition of cortical cultures, supported by VGAT expression data.

claim: SV-tag readily expresses in diverse brain areas, as evidenced by the abundance of tdTomato positive neurons in targeted regions.
source: SV-tag readily expresses in diverse areas, as evidenced by the abundance of tdTomato positive neurons in targeted regions (Figure 4B).
evidence: This observation is supported by immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Paired-pulse ratios were unaffected by SV-tag expression in presynaptic neurons at Schaffer collateral synapses.
source: Paired-pulse ratios, measured at an inter-stimulus interval of 50 ms, were unaffected by SV-tag expression in presynaptic neurons, which indicated that SV-tag did not significantly alter neurotransmitter release probability at this synapse (Figure S4C).
evidence: This electrophysiological finding is supported by data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Homogenizing the whole brain to immediately free SVs greatly improved yields compared to forming and lysing synaptosomes.
source: To resolve these issues, we compared several lysis protocols for their efficiency in releasing SVs from neurons. Compared to forming and lysing synaptosomes, homogenizing the whole brain to immediately free SVs greatly improved yields (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This methodological finding is supported by comparative data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The metabolite profiles of hippocampal SVs show glutamate and GABA detected with glutamate being the more abundant neurotransmitter.
source: The metabolite profiles of hippocampal SVs are expected, with glutamate and GABA detected and glutamate being the more abundant neurotransmitter (Figure 4D).
evidence: This finding is supported by LC/MS data presented in Figure 4D.

claim: No other metabolites other than glutamate and GABA were significantly present in hippocampal SVs.
source: Similar to cortical culture SVs, no other metabolites other than these two known neurotransmitters were significantly present.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the metabolomics analysis of hippocampal SVs.

claim: Striatal SVs from Slc32a1IRES-Cre mice reveal the enrichment of GABA and the concomitant depletion of glutamate.
source: Striatal SVs from Slc32a1IRES-Cre mice, where SV-tag expression is restricted to GABAergic neurons (Vong et al., 2011) and SVs from Adora2aCre mice, which restrict expression further to a subpopulation of GABAergic striatal neurons (Durieux et al., 2009; Figure 4—figure supplement 1G), reveal the enrichment of GABA and the concomitant depletion of glutamate (Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This finding is supported by LC/MS data presented in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1H, with citations for the mouse lines used.

claim: Cell-type specific expression of SV-tag permits analysis of SV content on material isolated directly from complex brain tissue.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that cell-type specific expression of SV-tag permits analysis of SV content on material isolated directly from complex brain tissue.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the successful cell-type-specific profiling experiments described.

claim: Substantia nigra SVs are enriched for dopamine and these stores are depleted by VMAT2 inhibition.
source: Using a modified LC/MS method for the detection of dopamine, we find that substantia nigra SVs are enriched for dopamine and these stores are depleted by VMAT2 inhibition (Figure 4I).
evidence: This finding is supported by targeted LC/MS data for dopamine presented in Figure 4I.

claim: Glutamatergic vesicles isolated from either cultured neurons or directly from the brain contain only glutamate and lack detectable amounts of other proposed neurotransmitters such as aspartate.
source: We find that glutamatergic vesicles, isolated from either cultured neurons or directly from the brain, contain only glutamate and lack detectable amounts of other proposed neurotransmitters (such as aspartate).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the comprehensive metabolomics analyses presented throughout the Results section.

claim: Untargeted analysis of polar metabolites failed to detect any additional molecule that was enriched within glutamatergic vesicles.
source: Indeed, untargeted analysis of polar metabolites failed to detect any additional molecule that was enriched within these vesicles.
evidence: This statement summarizes the findings from the global metabolomics screen.

claim: Dopamine was identified in SVs from substantia nigra neurons, but not GABA and glutamate, which are known to be released by these cells.
source: We were able to identify dopamine in SVs from substantia nigra neurons, but not GABA and glutamate (Tritsch et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2015), which are known to be released by these cells.
evidence: This observation is supported by the dopamine detection data and citations indicating that these cells also release GABA and glutamate.

claim: A robust GABA signal was observed in SVs from striatal cells but acetylcholine was not detected.
source: In addition, we observed a robust GABA signal in SVs from striatal cells but did not detect acetylcholine, which is released by a small population of interneurons that reside in this region (Cox and Witten, 2019).
evidence: This observation is based on the metabolomics data from striatal SVs, with a citation for the presence of cholinergic interneurons.

claim: Cholinergic neurons represent about 2% of striatal neurons.
source: As cholinergic neurons represent about 2% of striatal neurons (Zhou et al., 2002), this suggests a lower limit for the ability of our current protocol to detect minor neurotransmitters.
evidence: This quantitative statement is supported by a citation and is used to interpret the detection limits of the method.

claim: Neither aspartate nor taurine were enriched within SVs in the context of cultured neurons and the brain regions profiled in this study.
source: For instance, in the context of cultured neurons and the brain regions profiled in this study, neither aspartate nor taurine - molecules long debated to be neurotransmitters - were enriched within SVs, thus bringing into doubt their potential synaptic functions.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the absence of these metabolites in the comprehensive metabolomics analyses.

claim: Analysis in the hippocampus failed to find evidence in support of aspartate being a neurotransmitter.
source: Analysis in the hippocampus also failed to find evidence in support of aspartate being a neurotransmitter (Herring et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a study that reached the same conclusion.

claim: SVs are membrane-bound organelles located within presynaptic axon terminals.
source: Neurotransmitters are stored in synaptic vesicles (SVs), membrane-bound organelles located within presynaptic axon terminals and whose activity-dependent release is essential for proper transmission of information within the brain (Jahn and Südhof, 1994).
evidence: This is a foundational fact in neuroscience supported by a citation.

claim: The activity-dependent release of SVs is essential for proper transmission of information within the brain.
source: Neurotransmitters are stored in synaptic vesicles (SVs), membrane-bound organelles located within presynaptic axon terminals and whose activity-dependent release is essential for proper transmission of information within the brain (Jahn and Südhof, 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: Some neurotransmitters cause acute electrical activation or inhibition of a neuron by opening ion channels.
source: Whereas some neurotransmitters cause acute electrical activation or inhibition of a neuron by opening ion channels, others result in longer-term modulation of its signaling network by activating G-protein coupled receptors (Nicoll et al., 1990).
evidence: This statement describes established mechanisms of neurotransmitter action and is supported by a citation.

claim: Some neurotransmitters result in longer-term modulation of neuronal signaling by activating G-protein coupled receptors.
source: Whereas some neurotransmitters cause acute electrical activation or inhibition of a neuron by opening ion channels, others result in longer-term modulation of its signaling network by activating G-protein coupled receptors (Nicoll et al., 1990).
evidence: This statement describes established mechanisms of neurotransmitter action and is supported by a citation.

claim: Neurotransmitters were discovered more than a century ago.
source: Although neurotransmitters were discovered more than a century ago, our understanding of what molecules are used as neurotransmitters and how they change during life is likely incomplete.
evidence: This is a historical fact about the field of neuroscience.

claim: Our understanding of what molecules are used as neurotransmitters and how they change during life is likely incomplete.
source: Although neurotransmitters were discovered more than a century ago, our understanding of what molecules are used as neurotransmitters and how they change during life is likely incomplete.
evidence: This is the authors' assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Multiple neurotransmitters released by neurons may be packaged within the same or different SV pools or released from distinct axon terminals.
source: Further increasing the complexity, these neurotransmitters may be packaged within the same or different SV pools or released from distinct axon terminals (Hnasko and Edwards, 2012; Saunders et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to research describing these phenomena.

claim: Low mRNA and protein expression levels coupled with poor reagents for detection lead to false negatives and inaccurate conclusions when inferring neurotransmitter identity.
source: Low mRNA and protein expression levels coupled with poor reagents for detection lead to false negatives and inaccurate conclusions (Hnasko and Edwards, 2012).
evidence: This limitation of current methods is supported by a citation.

claim: Current approaches to infer neurotransmitter identity do not account for neurons that use unknown neurotransmitters or non-canonical pathways for neurotransmitter synthesis.
source: Moreover, these approaches do not account for neurons that use unknown neurotransmitters or non-canonical pathways for neurotransmitter synthesis (Kim et al., 2015; Tritsch et al., 2012).
evidence: This limitation is supported by citations to examples of non-canonical synthesis pathways.

claim: The substrate specificities for many neurotransmitter receptors and vesicular transporters remain unclear.
source: In addition, the substrate specificities for many neurotransmitter receptors and vesicular transporters remain unclear (Yelin and Schuldiner, 1995).
evidence: This statement about the current state of knowledge is supported by a citation.

claim: Many neurotransmitter receptors can be activated or allosterically modulated by diverse sets of small molecules that are found within cells.
source: However, many neurotransmitter receptors can be activated or allosterically modulated by diverse sets of small molecules that are found within cells, making this pharmacological approach difficult to interpret (Macdonald and Olsen, 1994; Patneau and Mayer, 1990).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations describing receptor promiscuity.

claim: Mass spectrometry is a powerful tool that identifies diverse metabolites in a systematic, sensitive and robust manner.
source: Many of these concerns can be addressed by direct profiling of SV contents using mass spectrometry (MS), a powerful tool that identifies diverse metabolites in a systematic, sensitive and robust manner (Patti et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement about MS capabilities is supported by a citation.

claim: MS has greatly expanded our understanding of organellar biology by providing insight into their rich and dynamic metabolomes.
source: Indeed, MS has greatly expanded our understanding of organellar biology by providing insight into their rich and dynamic metabolomes (Abu-Remaileh et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies using MS for organellar metabolomics.

claim: Current SV purification protocols are difficult to apply to specific neuronal populations in complex tissue.
source: More importantly, these protocols are difficult to apply to specific neuronal populations in complex tissue.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of existing methods that motivates the development of the new approach.

claim: The neurotransmitter profiles for diverse brain regions were characterized in a cell-type-specific manner using the developed workflow.
source: With this workflow, we characterized the neurotransmitter profiles for diverse brain regions in a cell-type- specific manner.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings of the study.

claim: The HA antibody is highly specific, sensitive, and well-characterized.
source: Furthermore, the HA antibody is highly specific, sensitive, and well-characterized.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of the HA antibody based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The SV-tag strategy enables the method to be generalizable as the HA-tag is easily appended to other proteins.
source: Finally, the SV-tag strategy enables this method to be generalizable as the HA-tag is easily appended to other proteins and is compatible with many other applications, including metabolic and proteomic studies (Chen et al., 2017; Huttlin et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement about the advantages of the approach is supported by citations to other studies using HA-tagging.

claim: A tdTomato sequence followed by a self-cleaving T2A sequence was appended to allow quick identification of infected cells via fluorescence.
source: In addition, we appended a tdTomato sequence followed by a self-cleaving T2A sequence to allow quick identification of infected cells via florescence.
evidence: This is a description of the construct design.

claim: For all approaches tested to improve targeting of SV-tag, the epitope tagged protein exhibited somatic localization comparable to that of SV-tag.
source: Surprisingly, for all of these approaches the epitope tagged protein exhibited somatic localization comparable to that of SV-tag (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This observation is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: It is difficult to achieve the correct level of expression for recombinant SV proteins to ensure that they are trafficked from the soma to the boutons.
source: This suggests that for recombinant SV proteins, it is difficult to achieve the correct level of expression to ensure that they are trafficked from the soma to the boutons.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed somatic localization of tagged proteins.

claim: A population of endogenous synaptophysin may be somatically localized but not accessible by the synaptophysin antibody.
source: Alternatively, it could indicate that a population of endogenous synaptophysin is somatically localized but not accessible by the synaptophysin antibody. This latter hypothesis is supported by the appearance of a somatic pool of synaptophysin when an HA-tag was introduced into the endogenous gene (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, top row).
evidence: This alternative hypothesis is supported by data from endogenous tagging experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The reduced porosity and magnetic properties of the beads used enable cleaner, quicker capture compared to standard agarose beads.
source: The reduced porosity and magnetic properties of these beads enable cleaner, quicker capture compared to standard agarose beads, which can trap metabolite contaminants within their porous bead matrix (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement about the advantages of the beads is supported by a citation.

claim: An extended tag of nine tandem HA sequences increased the yield of SVs despite expressing at a lower level than the triple HA-tag.
source: Indeed, an extended tag of nine tandem HA sequences increased the yield of SVs despite expressing at a lower level than the triple HA-tag (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This finding is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The most significantly enriched proteins in isolated SVs were SV resident proteins, including glutamate transporters, synaptobrevin, and vATPase subunits.
source: We also used mass spectrometry to profile the proteome of isolated SVs in depth and found that the most significantly enriched proteins were SV resident proteins, including glutamate transporters, synaptobrevin, and vATPase subunits (Supplementary file 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1E; Grønborg et al., 2010; Takamori et al., 2006).
evidence: This finding is supported by proteomics data and citations to established SV protein characterizations.

claim: Particles less than 40 nm observed in EM may be membrane fragments resulting from high-salt washes.
source: In addition, we observed particles less than 40 nm, which may be membrane fragments resulting from high-salt washes performed at the end of the isolation to reduce contaminants.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the EM observations.

claim: Larger particles (>100 nm) observed in EM may be large dense-core vesicles or contaminating organelles and cellular debris.
source: A minority of larger particles (>100 nm) are also present, which may be large dense-core vesicles (Gondré-lewis et al., 2012) or contaminating organelles and cellular debris.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the EM observations, with a citation for large dense-core vesicles.

claim: The 10-fold enrichment of SVs in the preparations is lower than the 20X enrichment reported for previous isolation methods.
source: This is lower than the 20X enrichment reported for previous isolation methods (Ahmed et al., 2013).
evidence: This comparison is made to a cited reference describing previous methods.

claim: It was not necessary to supplement ATP with magnesium in the isolation.
source: In our isolation, it was not necessary to supplement ATP with magnesium (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K), likely due to the rapidity of the method and/or sufficient levels of magnesium released during cell lysis to maintain vATPase function.
evidence: This observation is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1K and includes a speculative explanation.

claim: GC/MS has high sensitivity for many analytes, low cost and ease of operation.
source: To interrogate the metabolite contents of SVs in a precise and robust manner, we initially used targeted gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC/MS), a method with high sensitivity for many analytes, low cost and ease of operation, all of which are important considerations for optimization studies (Beale et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement about the advantages of GC/MS is supported by a citation.

claim: GC/MS is limited in its capacity to detect a wide range of polar metabolites, due to the need for polar metabolite volatilization and separation on a GC column.
source: Although GC/MS provides a strong starting point for analysis, it is limited in its capacity to detect a wide range of polar metabolites, due to the need for polar metabolite volatilization and separation on a GC column (Lei et al., 2011; Sobolevsky et al., 2003; Stenerson, 2011).
evidence: This limitation of GC/MS is supported by citations.

claim: LC/MS can detect a much broader range of metabolites with nanomolar sensitivity.
source: Therefore, we transitioned to metabolomic analysis by liquid chromatography – high-resolution mass spectrometry (LC/MS), which can detect a much broader range of metabolites with nanomolar sensitivity (Lei et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement about LC/MS capabilities is supported by a citation.

claim: Markers for other subcellular compartments were not enriched in SVs, including cystine (lysosomes), aspartate and phosphocholine (mitochondria).
source: Reflecting the specificity of our workflow for isolating SVs, markers for other subcellular compartments were not enriched, including cystine, which is characteristic of lysosomes (Pisoni and Thoene, 1991), and aspartate and phosphocholine, which are the most enriched metabolites in mitochondria (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This finding demonstrates the specificity of the isolation method and is supported by citations identifying these metabolites as organellar markers.

claim: Glutamate is imported into SVs via glutamate transporters VGLUT1 and VGLUT2.
source: To address this concern, we took advantage of the fact that glutamate is imported into SVs via glutamate transporters VGLUT1 and VGLUT2 (Takamori et al., 2001), which, unlike vATPase, are SV-specific proteins (Fremeau et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies characterizing these transporters.

claim: VGLUT1 and VGLUT2, unlike vATPase, are SV-specific proteins.
source: To address this concern, we took advantage of the fact that glutamate is imported into SVs via glutamate transporters VGLUT1 and VGLUT2 (Takamori et al., 2001), which, unlike vATPase, are SV-specific proteins (Fremeau et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Previous work has proposed that taurine, gamma-hydroxybutyrate, ß-alanine, and agmatine may function as neurotransmitters.
source: Previous work has proposed that other polar molecules may function as neurotransmitters, including taurine, gamma-hydroxybutyrate, ß-alanine, and agmatine (Cash, 1994; Davison and Kaczmarek, 1971; Kilb and Fukuda, 2017; Reis and Regunathan, 2000; Tiedje et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to studies proposing these molecules as neurotransmitters.

claim: The variability of the number of GABAergic interneurons across different cortical culture preps likely contributes to the variation in the GABA levels detected across MS runs.
source: The variability of the number of GABAergic interneurons across different cortical culture preps likely contributes to the variation in the GABA levels detected across MS runs.
evidence: This is an inference to explain observed variability in the data.

claim: Potassium arises from the putative pairing of this ion with carbonate ions in the LC buffers used in the IP/MS workflow.
source: In addition to GABA, we identified a peak that is associated with potassium, which arises from the putative pairing of this ion with carbonate ions in the LC buffers used in the IP/MS workflow.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the detection of potassium.

claim: Sample-to-sample fluctuations in potassium levels from reagents can contribute to altered potassium content.
source: However, potassium is a ubiquitous component of multiple reagents and sample-to-sample fluctuations in their levels can contribute to altered potassium content.
evidence: This is a caveat about the interpretation of potassium detection.

claim: Follow-up studies using atomic absorption spectroscopy or ICP-MS will be necessary to establish how much potassium SVs quantitatively contain.
source: Follow-up studies using atomic absorption spectroscopy or inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) will be necessary to establish how much potassium these SVs quantitatively contain, whether these weakly enriched potassium peaks are indeed internalized within SVs, and if they contribute to SV function.
evidence: This is a statement about future work needed to address limitations of the current study.

claim: In the brain, molecularly and functionally distinct neurons are intermingled in an intricate and heterogeneous environment.
source: However, in the brain, molecularly and functionally distinct neurons are intermingled in an intricate and heterogeneous environment, and they rely on the uptake of extracellular metabolites found in this environment for neurotransmitter synthesis (Elsworth and Roth, 1997; Mathews and Diamond, 2003; Schousboe et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations describing brain complexity and neurotransmitter synthesis.

claim: Neurons rely on the uptake of extracellular metabolites found in their environment for neurotransmitter synthesis.
source: However, in the brain, molecularly and functionally distinct neurons are intermingled in an intricate and heterogeneous environment, and they rely on the uptake of extracellular metabolites found in this environment for neurotransmitter synthesis (Elsworth and Roth, 1997; Mathews and Diamond, 2003; Schousboe et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: The expression of SV-tag was driven by the synapsin promoter to ensure neuron-specific expression.
source: To ensure neuron-specific expression, the expression of SV-tag was driven by the synapsin promoter (Kügler et al., 2003).
evidence: This methodological detail is supported by a citation for the synapsin promoter.

claim: Paired-pulse facilitation indicates changes in probability of release from presynaptic terminals.
source: Paired-pulse facilitation, which indicates changes in probability of release from presynaptic terminals, was assessed using pairs of closely spaced electrical stimuli (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an established electrophysiological measure used to assess synaptic function.

claim: Initial attempts to isolate SVs from brain tissue using the same strategy developed for cultured neurons resulted in preps with poor yield and high background.
source: Our initial attempts to isolate SVs from brain tissue using the same strategy developed for cultured neurons resulted in preps with poor yield and high background.
evidence: This describes an initial challenge that was subsequently addressed.

claim: A motorized homogenizer was necessary for effective and rapid lysis of brain tissue.
source: Importantly, a motorized homogenizer was necessary for effective and rapid lysis.
evidence: This is a methodological finding from optimization experiments.

claim: The addition of a final five-minute high-salt incubation after the IP reduced background contamination.
source: The addition of a final five-minute high-salt incubation after the IP further reduced background contamination.
evidence: This is a methodological finding from optimization experiments.

claim: These changes enabled SV isolation in under 30 min from diverse brain regions, including hippocampus, cortex, and striatum.
source: In combination, these changes enabled SV isolation in under 30 min from diverse brain regions, including hippocampus, cortex, and striatum (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a summary of the methodological achievements, supported by data in the referenced figures.

claim: SVs from brain tissue had minimal contamination of other subcellular organelles as demonstrated by immunoblot and electron microscope analyses.
source: Moreover, SVs had minimal contamination of other subcellular organelles as demonstrated by immunoblot and electron microscope analyses (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This finding is supported by immunoblot and EM data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The hippocampus is composed of roughly 90% glutamatergic pyramidal neurons and 10% GABAergic interneurons.
source: We profiled SVs from the hippocampus, which is composed of roughly 90% glutamatergic pyramidal neurons and 10% GABAergic interneurons (Olbrich and Braak, 1985), and the striatum, which is comprised primarily of GABAergic cells (Yoshida and Precht, 1971).
evidence: This statement about hippocampal composition is supported by a citation.

claim: The striatum is comprised primarily of GABAergic cells.
source: We profiled SVs from the hippocampus, which is composed of roughly 90% glutamatergic pyramidal neurons and 10% GABAergic interneurons (Olbrich and Braak, 1985), and the striatum, which is comprised primarily of GABAergic cells (Yoshida and Precht, 1971).
evidence: This statement about striatal composition is supported by a citation.

claim: Glutamate contamination in striatal SVs could result from isolation of SVs from glutamatergic cortical neurons that became infected with SV-tag due to pipette withdrawal and viral leak or via retrograde transduction.
source: Because SV-tag was expressed in a Cre-independent manner in wild-type mice, this could result from isolation of SVs from glutamatergic cortical neurons that lie above striatum and became infected with SV-tag due to pipette withdrawal and viral leak or via retrograde transduction due to axonal-uptake of AAV.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed glutamate contamination.

claim: Glutamate contamination in striatal SVs could be due to contamination by cortical and thalamic glutamatergic terminals that heavily innervate the striatum.
source: Alternatively, it could be due to contamination by cortical and thalamic glutamatergic terminals that heavily innervate the striatum.
evidence: This is an alternative speculative explanation for the observed glutamate contamination.

claim: Cre-expressing cells in Slc6a3IRES-Cre mice match well with the population of neurons that express VMAT2.
source: As has been previously demonstrated in the injection target, Cre-expressing cells in this mouse line match well with the population of neurons that express VMAT2, the vesicular dopamine transporter (Edwards, 1992; Lammel et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies characterizing this mouse line.

claim: Tetrabenazine is a reversible inhibitor of VMAT2.
source: In a cohort of mice expressing SV-tag, we administered tetrabenazine, a reversible inhibitor of VMAT2 (Erickson et al., 1996; Scherman et al., 1983), at a concentration validated to deplete dopamine from SVs in acute striatal slices (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I–J).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations describing tetrabenazine.

claim: The analyses of polar metabolites in SVs reveal that these organelles have a minimal metabolic content and contain only previously recognized bona fide neurotransmitters.
source: Our analyses of polar metabolites in SVs profiled in this study reveal that these organelles have a minimal metabolic content and contain only previously recognized bona fide neurotransmitters, which is consistent with their primary role in neurotransmitter storage and release.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the comprehensive metabolomics data presented.

claim: The minimal metabolic content of SVs is consistent with their primary role in neurotransmitter storage and release.
source: Our analyses of polar metabolites in SVs profiled in this study reveal that these organelles have a minimal metabolic content and contain only previously recognized bona fide neurotransmitters, which is consistent with their primary role in neurotransmitter storage and release.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the observed metabolic simplicity to known SV function.

claim: Zinc has been proposed to function as a neurotransmitter at excitatory synapses.
source: Indeed, zinc has been proposed to function as a neurotransmitter at excitatory synapses (Vergnano et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Further optimization of the immunocapture procedure to increase SV yields is necessary to utilize MS methods for atomic ion detection.
source: In addition, further optimization of the immunocapture procedure to increase SV yields is necessary to utilize MS methods for atomic ion detection, which require high amounts of starting material.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations and future directions.

claim: MS methods for atomic ion detection require high amounts of starting material.
source: In addition, further optimization of the immunocapture procedure to increase SV yields is necessary to utilize MS methods for atomic ion detection, which require high amounts of starting material.
evidence: This is a statement about the requirements of certain MS methods.

claim: The yield of SVs captured by the method and thus the detection limit would likely be increased by the use of a mouse line in which synaptophysin is endogenously tagged with HA in a conditional manner.
source: The yield of SVs captured by our method and thus the detection limit would likely be increased by the use of a mouse line in which synaptophysin is endogenously tagged with HA in a conditional manner.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential improvements to the method.

claim: Endogenous conditional tagging of synaptophysin would permit more uniform and complete expression of SV-tag in desired cells without ectopic overexpression.
source: This would permit more uniform and complete expression of SV-tag in desired cells without ectopic overexpression, and thus increase SV yields and the consistency between preps.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the advantages of endogenous tagging.

claim: Endogenous conditional tagging would eliminate the need for tedious injections and facilitate greater turnaround time of experiments.
source: Furthermore, it would eliminate the need for tedious injections and facilitate greater turnaround time of experiments.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about practical advantages of endogenous tagging.

claim: Loss of function experiments combined with global MS profiling will provide a powerful strategy to interrogate how SV2A and promiscuous vesicular transporters affect SV function.
source: Loss of function experiments combined with global MS profiling will provide a powerful strategy to interrogate how these proteins affect SV function.
evidence: This is a statement about potential future applications of the method.

claim: Only a fraction of SVs known as the rapidly releasable pool fuse upon electrical excitation of a neuron.
source: For instance, the release properties of SVs have long been known to be heterogeneous, and only a fraction of SVs known as the rapidly releasable pool fuse upon electrical excitation of a neuron (Rizzoli and Betz, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Proteomic profiling of different SV populations following immunoisolation could reveal the molecular basis for differences in release properties.
source: Proteomic profiling of these different SV populations following immunoisolation could reveal the molecular basis for these differences, which has long eluded researchers.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications.

claim: The method can facilitate the identification of neurons which corelease multiple transmitters.
source: Finally, this method can facilitate the identification of neurons which corelease multiple transmitters and follow-up studies with higher resolution methods such as EM or array tomography can address the basis of this corelease and if it occurs from the same or different vesicle.
evidence: This is a statement about potential applications of the method.

claim: The robustness and ease of the SV isolation and profiling methodology will serve as a platform to gain a deeper understanding of how SVs control neurotransmission.
source: In conclusion, the robustness and ease of our SV isolation and profiling methodology will serve as a platform upon which we can gain a deeper understanding of the diverse ways that these organelles control neurotransmission.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the significance and potential impact of the method.
